e: From Latin eiulātiō, from eiulō (“to wail, lament”).
q: Ejulation in the pangs of death.
1708, [John Philips], “Book II”, in Cyder. […], London: […] J[acob] Tonson, […], →OCLC, page 85:

e: Borrowed from Latin ēiūrātiō, from ēiūrō (“to abjure, disown, resign”) + -tiō.
q: Paul witnesseth of himself, before his conversion, to blaspheme, by their ejuration of the known truth, and their subscriptions to the Popish trumperies.
1645, Simonds D'Ewes, The primitive practise for preserving truth, page 12:
The Imperiall seat can not vaike but by death, or deprivation or eiuration[…]
1657, Alexander Petrie, A compendious history of the Catholick church from the year 600 untill the year 1600 shewing her deformation and reformation, page 54:
The Bishops of England after their conversion to the faith and ejuration of Papistry, have been the faithfull Servants of God[…]
